A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Projecting What a Tarik Skubal Contract Would Look Like From Mets
item.dc:creator: Logan VanDine; Unknown
item.description: When the 2026 MLB season ends following the World Series, all eyes will be on where two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal signs in the offseason. Skubal is expected to sign a record-setting contract this offseason, as the hard-throwing lefty has solidified himself as one of baseball's dominant starting pitchers. While many teams are expected to show interest in Skubal, the New York Mets should be right up there. For the second year in a row, starting pitching was an issue for New York a
item.content:encoded:
When the 2026 MLB season ends following the World Series, all eyes will be on where two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal signs in the offseason.
Skubal is expected to sign a record-setting contract this offseason, as the hard-throwing lefty has solidified himself as one of baseball's dominant starting pitchers. While many teams are expected to show interest in Skubal, the New York Mets should be right up there.
For the second year in a row, starting pitching was an issue for New York and was one reason they fell well short of expectations. If the Mets chose to pursue Skubal, what kind of contract would the ballclub offer the lefty hurler?
Why the Mets can afford Tarik Skubal
Six years after purchasing the Mets, Steve Cohen has proven he is willing to open his wallet and sign free agents to big contracts. One perfect example is when the Amazins' signed Juan Soto to a record-setting 15-year, $765 million deal in December 2024. I'm not saying the Mets would offer Skubal that type of contract, but they have shown in the past that they try to sign free-agent starters to huge deals.
During the 2023-2024 offseason, the Mets aggressively pursued Yoshinobu Yamamoto after the Nippon Professional Baseball League posted the Japanese phenom. The aforementioned Cohen and president of baseball operations David Stearns even traveled to Japan to meet him.
Yamamoto, of course, signed a 12-year, $325 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers and has since won two World Series and been named World Series MVP last season. While the Mets lost the Yamamoto pursuit to the Dodgers, Cohen and company have shown that when a prized free-agent starter is on the market, they will be interested.
Prediciting a Tarik Skubal Mets contract
In a recent article for SNY.tv, MLB insider Chelsea Janes reported a "general consensus" that if Cohen pursues Skubal in free agency, the Mets will pay "whatever it takes to get him."
To put that in perspective, recent starting-pitching free-agent contracts include Max Fried signing an eight-year, $218 million deal with the New York Yankees in December 2024.
Dylan Cease signed a seven-year, $210 million deal with the Toronto Blue Jays in December 2025, and Corbin Burnes inked a six-year, $210 million contract with the Arizona Diamondbacks in December 2024.
Skubal, a two-time AL Cy Young Award winner, has certainly proven to be one of the more dominant starting pitchers across baseball over the last couple of seasons. He may very well exceed the contracts Fried, Cease, and Burnes inked.
Given Skubal's success and the Mets signing Soto to a lucrative $765 million deal, it wouldn't be shocking if the lefty secured a 10-year, $350 million deal from New York. A contract like that would completely reset the market for starting pitchers, much like Soto's deal did. Soto's deal with the Mets also includes a no-trade clause, so it would not be a total shock if the Mets gave Skubal that as well
With the Mets in dire need of a veteran ace for the rotation and Cohen having proven of pursuing big-time free agents, Skubal seems like the perfect match.
Get Mets On SI straight to your inbox: sign up for our free newsletter here.
Logan VanDine is a contributing writer for On SI's Mets. Logan is a graduate of Rider University where he majored in Sports Media and minored in Sports Studies. During his time at Rider, Logan worked for Rider's radio station, 107.7 The Bronc as a sports host, producer and broadcaster, and for the school's paper: The Rider News. He began his time with The Rider News as a section writer for sports and was a copy editor for two years followed by being one of the sports editors during his senior year. Logan also placed third in the New Jersey Press Foundation Awards for sports feature writing. Aside from his work at On SI, he is also a writer for FanSided covering the New York Giants. He also previously wrote for Athlon Sports, covering the NFL and MLB.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers’ $182 Million Superstar Sends 2-Word Tarik Skubal Message Immediately After Exit
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers face a pivotal offseason after falling short of another World Series championship. Following their National League Championship Series elimination, the franchise must decide how to address an aging roster while keeping its championship window open. Several key players are approaching free agency, and the front office faces difficult decisions about which pieces to retain. The immediate challenge is figuring out how to respond to a disappointing finish after building a ros
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers face a pivotal offseason after falling short of another World Series championship.
Following their National League Championship Series elimination, the franchise must decide how to address an aging roster while keeping its championship window open. Several key players are approaching free agency, and the front office faces difficult decisions about which pieces to retain.
The immediate challenge is figuring out how to respond to a disappointing finish after building a roster capable of winning it all.
"For the first time in three years, the Dodgers' winter has begun with a quiet period," Jack Harris wrote for the New York Post. "They didn't reach the World Series this fall. Which means they have some time to sit back and take stock of their roster before the offseason kicks into gear."
One of the biggest decisions involves Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award ace acquired at the trade deadline who is now positioned to test free agency. And shortly after Los Angeles' season ended, one of its highest-paid stars made his feelings about Skubal's future clear.
Los Angeles Dodgers Star Sends Tarik Skubal Free Agency Message
Blake Snell, who signed a five-year, $182 million contract with Los Angeles ahead of the 2025 season, made a very concise recruiting pitch to Skubal immediately after the Dodgers were eliminated.
"Blake Snell made his pitch to Tarik Skubal as soon as the Dodgers were eliminated," Dodgers Nation reported. "His message, in his words: 'Don't leave.'"
The message reflects the relationship the two left-handed pitchers developed during Skubal's brief stint in Los Angeles. The Dodgers acquired Skubal at the trade deadline to strengthen their championship push, surrendering significant prospect capital for a chance to win another title.
Skubal's future remains uncertain, however, and his immediate reaction to the elimination offered little clarity about whether he would return.
"It was an honor and a privilege to be here and compete with these guys, and to wear L.A. across your hat and across your chest," Skubal said, according to the Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee. "It's something that I took a lot of pride in. And, obviously, didn't end the way that I wanted it to. But that's life. That's baseball. I had a ton of fun here, and I loved competing with these guys."
Can Los Angeles Dodgers Re-Sign Tarik Skubal This Offseason?
Skubal's availability presents Los Angeles with a major opportunity, but retaining him could require a record-setting investment. He is widely expected to surpass Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million record contract guarantee for a pitcher.
Snell's message makes the Dodgers' preference clear, but the decision ultimately rests with Skubal and the competing offers he receives. Los Angeles must determine whether committing substantial resources to its former deadline acquisition is the best way to address its roster needs.
After falling short of a third consecutive championship, the Dodgers have plenty of questions to answer. Bringing Skubal back could be one of the most consequential decisions of their offseason.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.content:encoded:
【MLB】大谷翔平のドジャースも影響? トランプ大統領がロックアウトを予測「起きるだろう」、ワールドシリーズは「誰も気にしていない」
北中米W杯抽選会での米国トランプ大統領。(Photo by Hector Vivas - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)
12月1日に労使協定が期限切れ。サラリーキャップ導入を巡り対立
アメリカのドナルド・トランプ大統領は10月20日、米大リーグ（MLB）で懸念されるロックアウトについて、「起きるだろう（That is going to happen）」との見通しを示した。一方、ワールドシリーズに関する質問には「誰も気にしていない（Nobody cares）」と答えた。米スポーツメディア『The Comeback』が報じた。
記者からロックアウトの可能性について尋ねられたトランプ大統領は、「そうなると思う。起きるだろう」と回答。その後、ワールドシリーズに進出したチームの年俸総額について質問されると、「分かった、また別の機会にしよう。誰も気にしていない」と述べたという。
MLBでは、球団側と選手会の現行労使協定が2026年12月1日に期限を迎える。次期協定を巡る大きな争点の一つが、サラリーキャップ（年俸総額の上限）の導入だ。球団側が導入を求める一方、選手会は反対している。
米メディア『アクシオス』も10月20日、今季のワールドシリーズがミルウォーキー・ブルワーズとタンパベイ・レイズの対戦となり、ロックアウトを巡る労使対立が焦点になっていると報じた。両チームは高額年俸を投じる球団とは異なる運営で勝ち上がっており、サラリーキャップ導入を巡る議論にも影響を与えている。
一方、大谷翔平が所属するロサンゼルス・ドジャースも、今後の労使交渉の影響を受ける可能性がある。ロックアウトに至れば、選手との契約や球団施設の利用などが制限され、オフシーズンの補強や2027年シーズンの準備に影響が及ぶことも考えられる。
トランプ大統領は以前からサラリーキャップの導入を支持する考えを示している。労使交渉が合意に至るかどうか、MLB各球団と選手会の動向が焦点となる。

item.content:encoded:
Mets rumors: Will New York pursue Tarik Skubal in free agency? appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Mets need to make some changes. New York wanted to compete this year but fell short of that goal to say the least. Overall, this Mets team has some legitimate uncertainty. Signing a superstar such as Tarik Skubal in MLB free agency would certainly represent a boost, but is New York even planning to pursue him this offseason?
"From my understanding… I think this is a deal that could happen if Steve Cohen wants it to happen," Chelsea Janes of SNY said. "… That doesn't mean Steve Cohen is running the team, it doesn't mean David Stearns doesn't have a say. I know that kind of gets muddled sometimes when we talk about this. But I think we all know that there are times when Steve Cohen enters the conversation and says look, 'You might not have done this because it was financially uncomfortable in another place. This might not be the player you would have pursued if you were really pinching pennies in Milwaukee, but here, we have the money.'"
Skubal was traded from the Detroit Tigers to the Los Angeles Dodgers before the 2026 deadline. The 29-year-old southpaw wasn't quite as dominant this past year as he was during his Cy Young seasons in 2024 and 2025, but he still pitched well. He missed time during the season due to injury as well. There isn't a team in baseball that would complain about a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts across 26 outings.

The Mets have been linked to many big-name free agents over the years, so it wouldn't be surprising to see them pursue Skubal.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers' Shohei Ohtani Admits He Was Exposed by Brewers in NLCS
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers' performance in the 2026 National League Championship Series was a stark contrast to their 2025 appearance. The Dodgers dominated every way they could in 2025 against the Milwaukee Brewers, sweeping them in four games. Before the 2026 NLCS, the Brewers vowed that this matchup would be different, and they backed that up. Milwaukee returned the favor, sweeping the back-to-back champions in dominant fashion. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' performance in the 2026 National League Championship Series was a stark contrast to their 2025 appearance.
The Dodgers dominated every way they could in 2025 against the Milwaukee Brewers, sweeping them in four games.
Before the 2026 NLCS, the Brewers vowed that this matchup would be different, and they backed that up. Milwaukee returned the favor, sweeping the back-to-back champions in dominant fashion.
It was a complete 180 in this year's NLCS, and that goes for Shohei Ohtani's play, too.
Ohtani struggled throughout the second half of the season, and those issues carried into the postseason. The 32-year-old had a difficult playoff run, with the Brewers exposing his struggles even further.
After the loss, Ohtani acknowledged that Milwaukee had "exposed" him and gave the Brewers credit for doing so.
"The Brewers were overall strong and a very good team, and it really exposed some of the parts of me as a player, and got to give some credit to that," Ohtani said through his interpreter.
Dodgers’ Hopes for Shohei Ohtani’s Recovery Fell Short in the Postseason
Ohtani hit .230 in the NLCS, getting a three-run home run in Game 4 and close to nothing else.
His overall postseason numbers were even worse, as he hit .192 with that one home run, three RBIs and an OPS of .631 while striking out 10 times in 26 at-bats over eight games.
The four-time MVP was a shell of himself, largely because of lingering injuries that weren't properly addressed during the regular season.
Ohtani was dealing with a combination of left knee irritation and right biceps tightness. His knee injury flared up in late June, and his right biceps tightness popped up multiple times throughout the year.
Ohtani's offensive decline began around mid-August and continued through his rough stretch into October. He didn't get enough time to return to his average form, as he played through those injuries until he hit the injured list in September.
The Dodgers hoped that those two weeks off would help him get to a better place, but that was more wishful thinking. Ohtani was never the same, and it was clear it hurt the Dodgers in the long run.
Will Shohei Ohtani Need Surgery to Address His Injuries?
Ohtani was noncommittal about potentially undergoing surgery this offseason.
“Hard to tell at this point,” he said. “It’s something that’s going to be analyzed, discussed over the offseason, and [we’ll] see if it’s a viable thing to do.”
What he did make clear, however, is that he plans on continuing his two-way play in 2027.

item.content:encoded:
ドジャースの大谷翔平は今季のレギュラーシーズン途中より、故障に悩まされ続けた。開幕から「二刀流」で出場し、投手では8勝（2敗）をマークするも、前半戦でマウンドを離れている。
【写真】ドジャース奥様会「今日も素敵なスマイル」の真美子さんをチェック　大谷翔平が今PS初本塁打！エール届いた
右上腕二頭筋の張り、さらに左膝も痛めたことで、7月3日のパドレス戦での先発が最後の登板となった。両箇所の故障はその後も長引き、投手での復帰を断念する決断も下され、さらに9月には試合欠場を経て、負傷者リスト（IL）に登録される事態に。シーズン残り5試合で復帰を果たした大谷は、今季の打撃成績を打率.275、30本塁打、81打点、OPS.889などの数字で終えている。
戦列復帰以降、ポストシーズンも含めバッティングも復調とはならず、ブルワーズとのナ・リーグ優勝決定シリーズ4戦目で58日ぶりとなる本塁打を放ったが、チームはシリーズ4連敗で敗退。予想外の苦戦は、主砲の不振も少なからず影響したことは間違いない。
チームの目標だった世界一3連覇を逃し、大谷自身も怪我で思うような結果を残せなかった今シーズン。メジャー公式サイト『MLB.com』では、10月19日配信の大谷の特集記事の中で、「オオタニは、重要な時期に打撃不振に陥ったドジャースの複数の打者の1人だった」と評している。さらに、その原因となった右腕、左膝の故障については、「球団側、そしてオオタニ自身も、もっと適切に対処できた可能性があったのでは」などと指摘。
同メディアは、「ドジャースは時折、オオタニの健康状態について先手を打った対応も取っていた。投手としての負担と打者としての負担を分けて管理したり、登板翌日には完全休養日を設けたりしていた」と球団側の対応を振り返る。だが、その一方で、「しかし、身体に明らかな問題が生じていることがはっきりするまでは、先発登板を回避させることも、負傷者リストに登録することもなかった」と訴えている。
不調を抱えていた大谷をシーズン終盤までプレーさせていた球団の判断に疑問を投げかける同メディアは、記事の最後で「もし、オオタニの今シーズンの結末を変えることができたとすれば、それは故障に苦しみ始めた初期の段階で、球団側がもっと積極的な対応を取ることだったのかもしれない」と結論付けている。
ポストシーズンでの戦いを終えた直後、大谷は引き続き二刀流でグラウンドに立つ意向を示していた。今季の苦い経験を踏まえ、ドジャースがどのようなコンディション管理を行うのかにも、大きな注目が集まる。
[文/構成:ココカラネクスト編集部]

By now, it's been like a week since the Los Angeles Dodgers were eliminated from the MLB playoffs.
That means the 2026 World Series is set, with the Milwaukee Brewers taking on the Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic.
Who knows how far the Los Angeles Dodgers could have gone in the MLB playoffs if Shohei Ohtani wasn't dealing with a handful of injuries/enduring a gnarly slump.
That said, Ohtani still took some time to send out a quick appreciation post.
More MLB on Heavy: Philadelphia Phillies Trade Prediction Lands 2X All-Star Outfielder
Shohei Ohtani Makes Quick Social Media Post
In the week following the Los Angeles Dodgers' elimination from the MLB playoffs, Shohei Ohtani made the following 2-word appreciation post, with the caption:
"Thank you"
Some fans in the comments are very glad/excited that Shohei Ohtani is finally able to get some rest, as the past three years have been Go, Go, Go for Ohtani.
It's been reported that Ohtani has been dealing with a knee/biceps injury during 2026, and there's a possibility that Ohtani will undergo offseason surgery.
More MLB on Heavy: Ex-New York Yankees Pitcher Still a Free Agent Following Release

item.title: [www.the-sun.com] Dodgers star sends message to fans as World Series hero enters free agency
item.dc:creator: Ricky Westaby
item.description: A LOS Angeles Dodgers star has sent a message to the fans after the World Series hero entered free agency. The Dodgers were denied a chance at three consecutive World Series titles this year after they were brutally swept in the NLCS. In a somewhat shocking affair, the Milwaukee Brewers got out the broom and brushed aside a $340 million payroll outfit inside three. Just hours after the Brewers returned to the World Series for the first time since 1982, Dodgers hero Miguel Rojas announced his ret
item.content:encoded:
A LOS Angeles Dodgers star has sent a message to the fans after the World Series hero entered free agency.
The Dodgers were denied a chance at three consecutive World Series titles this year after they were brutally swept in the NLCS.
In a somewhat shocking affair, the Milwaukee Brewers got out the broom and brushed aside a $340 million payroll outfit inside three.
Just hours after the Brewers returned to the World Series for the first time since 1982, Dodgers hero Miguel Rojas announced his retirement.
And now it seems like more core members of the Dodgers’ back-to-back crew will be on their way out of LA.
The Dodgers have a number of stars hitting free agency, with star reliever Alex Vesia one of them.
READ MORE ON BASEBALL
After superstar pitcher Tarik Skubal, there is no player whose departure will hit harder than Vesia’s.
He has been an integral part of the Dodgers bullpen since 2021, but he has no idea whether he will be returning for the 2027 MLB season.
Vesia, 30, took to his Instagram to share a message with the Dodgers fanbase after their troubling defeat to the Brewers.
“By far the hardest year of my career. It’s hard to put into words what this season was like,” Vesia wrote in his Instagram caption.
How to watch the MLB post-season
MLB has new national TV deals for 2026-28 with ESPN, NBCUniversal, and Netflix. Several elements of MLB's national broadcast rights have not changed, including Fox, Warner Bros., and Apple Inc. deals for national coverage.
NBC returned to regular broadcast MLB coverage for the first time in 25 years. And Netflix made yet another significant move into live event coverage.
NBC: Sunday Night Baseball (moving from ESPN), Sunday Leadoff Games, whole Wild Card series, Labor Day primetime games and Opening Day primetime games
Netflix: Opening Night exclusive game, T-Mobile Home Run Derby, MLB at Field of Dreams Game (Beginning 2026), World Baseball Classic in Japan
ESPN: National midweek game package (30 games), secured the rights to sell and distribute MLB.TV into the ESPN app
*If you click on a link below, we will earn affiliate revenue
- CLICK HERE to subscribe to Peacock
- CLICK HERE to subscribe to ESPN
- CLICK HERE to subscribe to MLB TV
“Personal battles with confidence, expectations and highs and lows mentally.
“I can’t thank my teammates enough for picking me up on down days and dealing with my crazy ass on my high ones.
“I don’t know what the future holds, but I do want to say thank you to Dodger Nation for showing me so much love over the past 6 years, especially this year. I’m just a man on a mission!”
Following his 2024 World Series heroics, allowing only one hit and one walk while striking out two in 2 and two-third scoreless innings, the next season was a tremendously tough one for Vesia.
He and his wife Kayla lost their newborn daughter right before the 2025 World Series in October that year, which he sat out of as a result.
Showing how much he meant to the team, Vesia’s teammates paid tribute by having his number 51 stitched into their caps for the World Series.
Despite his tough off-the-field situation, the 30-year-old bounced back with a 2.64 ERA across 72 appearances this season.
Vesia would certainly be missed by all of Dodgers nation should he be allowed to walk this offseason.

item.title: [purplerow.com] Tuesday Rockpile: What TJ Rumfield’s defense brings to the Rockies
item.dc:creator: Renee Dechert
item.description: Last week, Rawlings announced their 2026 Gold Glove Finalists. Perhaps surprising to some (but not Colorado Rockies fans) was the inclusion of Rockies first baseman TJ Rumfield along with Matt Olson and Ty France. “It’s not easy to do in your first year,” said Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer via a phone call last week. Of Rumfield’s defense, Schaeffer said, “It was impressive, and it was steady.” Rumfield became one of five rookies since 1901 to have a season with at least 1,150 innings at firs
item.content:encoded:
Last week, Rawlings announced their 2026 Gold Glove Finalists. Perhaps surprising to some (but not Colorado Rockies fans) was the inclusion of Rockies first baseman TJ Rumfield along with Matt Olson and Ty France.
“It’s not easy to do in your first year,” said Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer via a phone call last week.
Of Rumfield’s defense, Schaeffer said, “It was impressive, and it was steady.”
Rumfield became one of five rookies since 1901 to have a season with at least 1,150 innings at first base and have seven or fewer errors, joining Todd Helton (1998), Travis Lee (1998, ARI), Freddie Freeman (2011, ATL), and Nolan Schanuel (2024, LAA).
It’s worth considering, then, how he compares defensively with his fellow finalists as well as what he brings to a rebuilding Rockies team.
Considering the competition
“TJ, I think, has always been a fairly underrated prospect,” said Amir Mamdani, Rockies director of baseball operations, via text message. “I think in part because he doesn’t meet the archetype of a typical 1B slugger.”
He continued, “I think TJ’s gift, which we were fortunate to see on display for 155 games, is the fact that he has a tremendous feel to hit. Has always put the ball in play at an impressive rate, and while the power has been more modest (15-20 HR a season), he’s always held his own offensively as he moved up through New York’s system, and ultimately seemed pretty blocked there, behind Ben Rice, Paul Goldschmidt, and others.”
The Rockies were happy to take advantage of the Yankees surplus.
In 2026, Rumfield saw his first year of MLB play, and he made the most of it. Matt Olson of the Atlanta Braves is 32 and is already a three-time Gold Glove winner. San Diego Padre Ty France, also 32, has won a Gold Glove as well.
Rumfield is the only newbie of the group, and while he did win an MiLB Gold Glove for first base in 2023, this announcement is another way to announce the rookie’s arrival.
Now to the numbers.
Here’s how the three finalists compare defensively in terms of standard defensive metrics as shown by FanGraphs:
Olson has played significantly more defensive innings (1424.0) than Rumfield (1156.1), and both are well ahead of France (1030.1). Although Olson has one more error than Rumfield, given the number of innings he logged, it’s difficult to hold that against him. Olson also started and finished more double plays than either of the other finalists. By this metric, Olson has clearly made a case for his fourth Gold Glove.
Although France leads the trio in defensive runs saved, Olson again has the better numbers in terms of outs above average and fielding run value.
Rumfield had a 2026 that placed him (rightfully) in the Rookie of the Year conversation, but the numbers indicate that he is not a Gold Glove front runner.
Still, it’s been a tremendous season for the Rockies first baseman.
“For him to be mentioned among Matt Olson and Ty France,” Schaeffer said, “those are two really good defenders, and I’m proud of TJ for the work he put in every day to get there.”
Considering what he brings to the Rockies
Schaeffer is quick to acknowledge what Rumfield means for Colorado.
“For a big man over there, which a lot of first basemen are, his hands are soft,” Schaeffer said, “and he makes pretty much every play over there — difficult plays.”
And it’s not just the plays that Rumfield makes; it’s also how he anchors his infield teammates.
“He’s got the athletic ability to read hops,” Schaeffer said, “and for me as an infielder myself, the the biggest thing for a first baseman was giving the rest of the infielders confidence that you can make a great play and not make the best throw, and your guy’s going to pick you up over there, and TJ does that on a consistent basis.”
Schaeffer added, “I think he makes life easy, way easier for [Ezequiel] Tovar and for [Kyle] Karros, and for whoever was playing second base — Willi Castro — and they know that. So they can try to make more difficult plays because they know that he’s going to pick them up on the backside.”
Rockies general manager Josh Brynes agrees.
“I thought receiving throws, like the wingspan picks, all that stuff, it felt like he saved a lot of errors or converted outs,” Brynes said over the phone, adding, “Just the infielders, their freedom of making any kind of throw is enhanced.”
Although the rebuilding Rockies are coming off a less-than-stellar season defensively, Rumfield was a stalwart at first, which Schaeffer sees as key for any successful defensive unit.
“I mean, (if) you have a really good first baseman, you can do more things. Kyle Karros can try more crazy plays where you have to be free to do it. And if you have any inkling that your first baseman isn’t going to catch the ball, you can’t make those plays. And same thing with Tovar on that side of the on that side of the diamond,” Schaeffer noted.
He pointed to other MLB first basemen to illustrate his point.
“When Christian Walker was in Arizona, he anchored that good infield that they had. Matt Olson anchors that infield. Even Freddie Freeman in L.A — they throw it over there, and they know he’s going to catch everything. So you see really good infields anchored by first basemen that receive every throw.”
Mamdani concurs.
“Defensively, I think it’s a credit to him and all the work he’s put in,” Mandani said.
“He and Andy González worked a lot this year, whether it be the red machine, or other defensive drills, and I think if you look at his contribution both from a statistical standpoint with range and defensive runs saved, but even in terms of his receiving at first base. The number of plays he made, even anecdotally, to make scoops, or catch balls as a big target that other first basemen wouldn’t be able to get to, he was just incredibly steady over there, and I’m happy for him that that’s being recognized.”
Even if Rumfield isn’t a Gold Glove winner in 2026, that’s some high praise, and he’s set himself up to build on this year going forward.
”It’s a testament to him and the work that he put in, because I think (with) defense, there’s skill involved certainly, but a lot of it is sort of effort and practice and focus,” said Ian Levin, Rockies assistant general manager of baseball operations, over the phone.
“And he puts in the time, he puts in the effort, and he’s done it throughout his career prior to coming to us, and then we see it with us. So, just the the ability for him to to do that, put into action, and now actually become a Gold Glove finalist for it, I think is huge credit.”
“Just to be a finalist, that’s awesome as a rookie to be among those (players),” Schaeffer said. “TJ, he set a high bar for himself in his first year.”
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on November 1, 2026.
This story was updated to include comments from Rockies general manager Josh Byrnes.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] How Dodgers can best utilize Josue De Paula with Shohei Ohtani problem
item.dc:creator: Conor Liguori

For the first time since 2023, the Los Angeles Dodgers will not be crowned Major League Baseball's champion. Surely, the NL West organization will be looking to end up back on top next year with a few minor roster adjustments. Most of the Dodgers' roster is expected back in 2027, including, of course, Shohei Ohtani at desig
item.content:encoded:
How Dodgers can best utilize Josue De Paula with Shohei Ohtani problem originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
For the first time since 2023, the Los Angeles Dodgers will not be crowned Major League Baseball's champion.
Surely, the NL West organization will be looking to end up back on top next year with a few minor roster adjustments.
Most of the Dodgers' roster is expected back in 2027, including, of course, Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter.
Top prospect Josue De Paula could play a larger role, but the Dodgers may have to clear space in the outfield.
"There admittedly isn't much that the Los Angeles Dodgers can do other than hope for better years from their core position players, but one thing they can and really must do is clear room for Josue De Paula," FanSided's Zachary Rotman wrote.
"DH is probably De Paula's best position, but with Shohei Ohtani taking up that spot for the long-term future (and rightfully so), the Dodgers need to find room for their 21-year-old phenom in the corner outfield," he added.
In a small sample size of 42 plate appearances, De Paul hit .323 with a homer and three doubles. Facing MLB pitching for the first time, he walked six more times (11) than he struck out (5).
Rotman suggested the Dodgers contemplate moving on from one of their corner outfielders, but it probably won't be Kyle Tucker.
"Many Dodgers fans would probably love for the team to trade Kyle Tucker away after his wildly disappointing debut season in L.A., but given his contract, the odds of that happening are slim to none," Rotman wrote. "That leaves Teoscar Hernandez as the player likeliest to get dealt, or at least placed in a short-side platoon role, with De Paula playing most of the time against right-handed pitching."
If the Dodgers can find a trade suitor for Hernandez, that would leave De Paula as their likely everyday left fielder and more room for the 21-year-old to grow.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Tigers Can Have Tarik Skubal Back at a Record Price
item.dc:creator: Glenn Kaplan
item.description: The Detroit Tigers traded starting pitcher Tarik Skubal to the Los Angeles Dodgers for outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith on Aug. 1, a day and a half before the 2026 MLB trade deadline. Skubal was playing out the final year of his contract on a $32 million arbitration salary, and the Tigers wanted to get something back rather than watch him leave for nothing. The question now is what kind of pay day he gets on the open market. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 mi
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Tigers traded starting pitcher Tarik Skubal to the Los Angeles Dodgers for outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith on Aug. 1, a day and a half before the 2026 MLB trade deadline. Skubal was playing out the final year of his contract on a $32 million arbitration salary, and the Tigers wanted to get something back rather than watch him leave for nothing.
The question now is what kind of pay day he gets on the open market. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million deal with the Dodgers is still the largest guarantee ever handed to a pitcher, and the projections on Skubal all start right about there. So this is not really a question of whether Detroit wants him back. It is a question of whether the Tigers will beat the biggest contract any pitcher has ever signed.
What a Tarik Skubal contract would cost the Detroit Tigers
ESPN's Kiley McDaniel surveyed 27 industry insiders on Oct. 2, and the average projection came back at eight years and $355 million, a $44.6 million average annual value. Sixteen of the 27, or 59 percent, landed between $325 million and $400 million over seven to 10 years. The full spread ran from four years and $176 million to 10 years and $500 million. SI's Tigers site put the number in that same $325 million to $400 million window.
Twenty-one of those 27 panelists expect Skubal to sign before Dec. 1, when the current collective bargaining agreement expires. The Dodgers and the New York Mets were named as true contenders, with the New York Yankees close behind and the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and San Diego Padres listed as sleepers. Detroit was on the contender list too, which is the one part of this that should give Tigers fans something to hold onto.
Detroit already declined to pay him once
This is the hard part of the argument. Tigers president of baseball operations Scott Harris said after the deadline that the club had approached Skubal and his camp about an extension at one point, and that it was made clear to him Skubal wanted to reach free agency.
"Which is totally his right, and nobody should be upset about that," Harris said. He called it irresponsible not to move Skubal given the market for him, and he put the season on himself: "It's not on the players. It's not on the coaches. It's on me."
So a front office that would not get an extension done, and then traded him for prospects, is now being asked to outbid the Dodgers and the Mets at full price. Detroit does not just have to find the money. It has to explain the reversal.
Framber Valdez set the current Tigers ceiling
Detroit's largest pitching commitment is Framber Valdez, who signed a three-year, $115 million deal in February. His $38.3 million average annual value set a record for left-handed pitchers, and he can opt out after the second season. He was brought in to slot behind Skubal, and he is the top of the rotation now by default.
That is a real commitment. It is also not in the same conversation as $355 million over eight years. If the Tigers want to put a second front-line arm next to Valdez, Skubal is the best one available, and he is also the most expensive player on the board by a wide margin.
What the Tigers would be paying for
Skubal made 26 starts in 2026 between Detroit and Los Angeles and went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA. He threw 158 2/3 innings, gave up 126 hits and 52 runs, walked 27 and struck out 186, and finished with a 0.96 WHIP. He is 29 and turns 30 on Nov. 20, so the longest deals on the board would run deep into his 30s.
It would still be a major surprise if the Tigers gave Skubal a record-breaking contract. The money sits outside anything Detroit has shown it will spend on one player, and Harris already walked away from a smaller version of this decision. Someone is going to pay Skubal. Going on what the Tigers have already done, it is hard to see it being them.

item.title: [abc7.com] Where 2026 ranks among best World Series matchups since 2000
item.dc:creator: David Schoenfield
item.description: This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played. The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS,
item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.
]

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Roberts Says Brewers Won the At-Bats in Dodgers' Game 2 Loss
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts gave Milwaukee credit for the work that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole. After Monday’s 7–4 loss, he pointed to the Brewers’ longer at-bats, contact and ability to create trouble on the bases. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts gave Milwaukee credit for the work that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole. After Monday’s 7–4 loss, he pointed to the Brewers’ longer at-bats, contact and ability to create trouble on the bases. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s early exit forced Roberts to cover more than six innings with his bullpen, and two leads slipped away. With the series heading to Los Angeles, Roberts wants length from Blake Snell and more help from the lineup.
A rare rough outing for Yamamoto
Roberts saw Yamamoto struggle to find his usual sharpness, with the third inning pushing his pitch count toward an early exit.
“He wasn’t sharp today,” Roberts said. “You can see from that Contreras at-bat in the third inning that really stressed him. You’ve got to give him a lot of credit. Then you follow that up with the Bauers at-bat, and the pitch count certainly crept up.”
“At that point, you’ve got Yelich, call it 70 pitches, and you’re trying to think about maybe getting him through it, as one of your guys, to shorten the game and give us a little bit of length.”
Yelich’s two-run single ended Yamamoto’s afternoon after 2⅔ innings.
“Once Yelich gets a hit, we’ve got to find a way to put it out and give ourselves a chance,” Roberts said. “He just didn’t have it tonight, which is very rare.”
Asked about close pitches to Brice Turang that went unchallenged, Roberts explained why those calls rest with the players.
“Will’s got a great view back there, as all catchers do,” he said. “As an offense, you try to defer to the hitter to save those challenges, defer to the catcher to save those challenges. In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike.”
“If you look back and that’s a called third strike, he doesn’t double, and that changes the outing. But I’m not back there. You’ve got to trust the players to make those decisions when they get in those spots.”
Why Sasaki pitched one inning
Roki Sasaki worked a scoreless fourth before Roberts turned to Kris Bubic in the fifth. Roberts said the run of left-handed hitters made that a spot he wanted for Bubic.
“You’re trying to cover six-plus innings,” he said. “I felt Bubic, you get four out of five left-handed hitters, and that’s a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren’t going to hit for them.”
“You’ve got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy where, in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic. He tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras, and then he hits a homer.”
“That’s a decision I made. That’s his lane, to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
Contreras’ homer tied the game. In the sixth, Roberts stayed with Brock Stewart to face him, hoping for a ground ball with runners at first and third.
“I felt like we had a chance to put him on the ground, get a double-play ball,” Roberts said. “Contreras didn’t hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that’s what they do.”
Milwaukee creates the trouble
The Brewers finished with 12 hits to the Dodgers’ three. Roberts felt the gap began with how the teams handled their at-bats.
“They saw a ton more pitches than we did. And they had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom,” he said. “They put the ball in play, created havoc. That’s the difference in the game.”
Asked about the Dodgers’ struggles against Milwaukee’s bullpen, Roberts included the starter in his assessment.
“We had three hits tonight. It was some of the starter, some of the bullpen,” he said. “They’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re finding ways to win pitches better than we are.”
“Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit. There were a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
Snell gets the next chance
Roberts wants Snell to give the Dodgers a longer start in Game 3, allowing the bullpen to work with a lead.
“We need Snell to go out there and give us some length, give us a typical Blake Snell outing,” he said. “I know Blake has a bad taste in his mouth from that last outing against the Braves. You’re going to see a locked-in, focused Snell.”
“On the other side of things, we’ve got to support him offensively, too.”
Roberts still sees a path back into the series, starting with one win at home.
“If you look at Game 3, I like where we’re at as far as who’s pitching, where our bullpen is at, being at home,” he said. “Then you’ve got to go from there.”
“Can we do it? Absolutely. You want to get that first one.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Skubal & Kiké Headlight Dodgers 2027 Free Agent Class
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers. After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers.
After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season.
While the list reads as nine, it is essentially eight, as veteran infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers’ Game Four loss.
Free Agents
(9): Blake Treinen, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Alex Vesia, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Tarik Skubal
Blake Treinen
Veteran right-hander Blake Treinen’s season ended during the final week of September after a right shoulder setback that forced him off the Dodgers postseason roster.
Treinen returned to Los Angeles after his 2024 World Series heroics on a 2-year, $14 million contract, and now the 38-year-old will be without a home entering an offseason that may be the final season of his career.
Evan Phillips
Right-hander Evan Phillips missed all of 2025 and returned toward the middle of the 2026 regular season due to Tommy John surgery. However, in his games played, he was very effective, going 3-2 with a 3.46 ERA.
Still, Phillips will be entering his age 33 season and has already missed significant time due to right elbow/arm injuries, and with multiple pitchers in the pipeline, it’s not hard to see the Dodgers moving on.
Kris Bubic
Acquired at the trade deadline, left-hander Kris Bubic is likely to get a contract this Winter as a starter, since that was his primary role before injuries derailed his 2026 season.
Bubic was an All-Star in 2025 and, with a thin free-agent market, could land a nice contract from a team desperate for starting pitching.
Miguel Rojas
Shortly after the conclusion of Game Four of the NLCS, veteran utility infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball, bringing an end to his 13-year playing career.
Rojas is expected to remain with the Dodgers organization in a player devleopment/coaching role.
Kiké Hernández
October hero Kiké Hernández is hitting free agency yet again this Winter, and after a subpar performance in October, minus one huge home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS, not much is known about whether the Dodgers will try to run it back for another 1-year deal.
Overall, Hernández missed most of the season while recovering from elbow surgery and an oblique injury and hit 4 home runs in 90 at-bats while posting a below-average 82 OPS+.
The fan favorite will enter his age-36 season, likely ending his Dodgers tenure for the second time.
Alex Vesia
Arguably the biggest free agent from the Dodgers bullpen this Winter is left-hander Alex Vesia, who has likely pitched his way to a sizable multi-year contract that the Dodgers might not be inclined to match.
Vesia, 30, posted an elite 2.64 ERA and struck out 74 batters despite a below-average fastball velocity, but with backend pitching at a premium, his market is likely to be heavy.
Brusdar Graterol
Brusdar Graterol’s career has been defined by injuries, and that likely will force his time in Dodger Blue to come to an end this Winter.
Despite a 2.78 career ERA, the right-hander has pitched only 7.1 innings for the Dodgers since the 2024 regular season, missing the entire 2025 and 2026 seasons due to right shoulder surgery.
Eric Lauer
Like Bubic, left-hander Eric Lauer will enter the market as a starting pitcher, and after a second-half renaissance with the Dodgers, where he went 7-2 with a 4.50 ERA, he could be a dependable backend starter to eat innings for a variety of clubs.
Tarik Skubal
The consensus No. 1 free agent this Winter across baseball is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is set to demand a massive multi-year contract that could go north of $400 million.
While the Dodgers will no doubt be involved, it’s hard to imagine them matching that while already having so many long-term deals tied up, especially in their starting rotation already.
Skubal is likely to sign before the MLB lockout on December 1st to maximize his contract, such as fellow Scott Boras client Corey Seager did after the 2021 season.

Cody Snavely has been the co-editor of DodgersBeat and full-time host of the Bleed Los Podcast since February 2023. He has also written for multiple websites, such as Dodgers Way, Dodgers Low-Down, and Dodgers Tailgate. A Wilmington University graduate, Snavely is an avid Dodgers fan who uses his advanced baseball knowledge to keep fans updated on the latest storylines, rumors, and opinions on Dodgers baseball.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] The end of the Yankees dynasty could be telling for Dodgers, Dave Roberts’ future
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Empires crumble, dynasties fade, and new powers emerge. The only thing consistent through history is change, which is something that the Los Angeles Dodgers will come to learn sooner or later. Whether the sweep the Dodgers suffered at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers was a temporary setback or the beginning of the end remains to be seen. Regardless, the end is coming at some point, and that will put Dave Roberts in an uncomfortable position. Tyler Kepner of The Athletic covered the New York Ya
item.content:encoded:
Empires crumble, dynasties fade, and new powers emerge. The only thing consistent through history is change, which is something that the Los Angeles Dodgers will come to learn sooner or later. Whether the sweep the Dodgers suffered at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers was a temporary setback or the beginning of the end remains to be seen.
Regardless, the end is coming at some point, and that will put Dave Roberts in an uncomfortable position. Tyler Kepner of The Athletic covered the New York Yankees during the end of their famous dynasty in the early 2000s and put together some lessons the Dodgers will learn from history.
The first big key is the fact that the league doesn't like dynasties. MLB updated the Competitive Balance Tax during the 2002 CBA negotiations, introducing the first version of the repeat offender tax in an attempt to stop the Yankees, who clearly felt that the tax itself was no barrier to their big-spending ways. Los Angeles faces a similar, but more stringent obstacle coming down the pike, with the league now pushing for an outright salary cap.
Whether or not that actually comes to fruition and slows down the Dodgers remains to be seen. What is for sure is the fact that the run will eventually come to an end, and it will mean the end for Roberts.
Sooner or later, Dave Roberts will become a Los Angeles Dodgers scapegoat
During the late 1990s and early 2000s, New York was led by Joe Torre. Torre wasn't a legendary manager at the time. The former catcher came to the Yankees with a .471 winning percentage over 14 years as a manager and had never won a playoff game. He might have been hired because Yankees owner George Steinbrenner believed he could control the undistinguished skipper.
Torre won the World Series in his first season at the helm, with the Yankees serving as the upstart against the more established Atlanta Braves. He'd suffer an early exit from the postseason in 1997, but his club would come back and go on a rampage in 1998 with a whopping 114 wins and a second ring for Torre. He'd then win two more to complete the three-peat, while making the Fall Classic, but coming up short in 2001 and 2003.
Torre's final three years with New York featured first-round playoff exits, and while the Yankees never actually fired him, they offered him only a one-year contract with a pay cut following the 2007 season.
The dirty little secret is that Torre wasn't really the reason that New York entered a championship drought. Instead, the organization moved away from what originally made it successful. The Yankees were built on a foundation that was called the Core Four — homegrown heroes Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Jorge Posada, and Andy Pettitte. The name is a misnomer because, in reality, Bernie Williams, also a homegrown star, who just happened to be a couple of years older than the others, was an integral part of their success.
Supporting that core were a bunch of savvy pickups. Paul O'Neill was a platoon bat who frequently clashed with Lou Piniella in Cincinnati, but became the fearsome No. 3 hitter in the Yankees' order. Tino Martinez was a similar sort of player who was pushed out of Seattle and became a fearsome slugger with New York. Scott Brosius became the defensive whiz with a penchant for the clutch hit after being rescued from Oakland. The list goes on.
However, after the 2001 heartbreak at the hands of the Arizona Diamondbacks, the Yankees saw two things happen. Key players aged, and rather than finding young, up-and-coming stars as they had before, they spent like a drunken sailor in free agency, bringing in guys like Jason Giambi and Gary Sheffield. What ended up happening is they paid a premium for past performance, and while many of these pickups weren't bad, they were on the decline.
Rather than have general manager Brian Cashman or Steinbrenner face the music, Torre was the easy scapegoat.
At the end of the day, the league will try to make it harder for a dynasty to continue leveraging whatever it was that gave it an advantage. Meanwhile, the rest of the teams will start emulating you, reducing the value of what originally set you apart. And while a manager has a lot of responsibility for what happens on the field, he ultimately is the low man on the totem pole in the leadership hierarchy.
Roberts can't control how players age. He can't control how Andrew Friedman adds to the roster. He can't control what MLB does to legislate the Dodgers' advantage out of the game. And he'll eventually learn the same fate that Torre learned.
The Dodgers will still win a lot of games, but these external factors will keep them from reaching the summit, and he'll get the pink slip before anyone else is held accountable for the deterioration of the Los Angeles juggernaut.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Hyeseong Kim apologizes to Dodgers fans for disappointing season
item.dc:creator: Blake Williams
item.description: During Spring Training, Hyeseong Kim was in the running to be the Los Angeles Dodgers’ starting second baseman while Tommy Edman was out. Instead, the job went to Alex Freeland. Kim opened the year in Triple-A and didn’t spend much time with the Dodgers. He appeared in just 43 games and didn’t produce much when given the opportunity.
